source.text: Μετὰ ταῦτα ἀπῆλθεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς Γαλιλαίας τῆς Τιβεριάδος.

records.literal_gloss: After these things went away the Jesus across the sea of the Galilee of the Tiberias.

en.L: After these things Jesus went off across the Sea of Galilee, [the Sea] of Tiberias.
en.B: Some time later Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias.
en.R: After this, Jesus went across to the other side of the Sea of Galilee. This large lake was also called the Sea of Tiberias.

es.L: Después de estas cosas, Jesús se fue al otro lado del mar de Galilea, [el mar] de Tiberíades.
es.B: Algún tiempo después, Jesús se fue al otro lado del mar de Galilea, que también se llama mar de Tiberíades.
es.R: Después de esto, Jesús cruzó al otro lado del mar de Galilea. Este gran lago también se llamaba mar de Tiberíades.

decisions.choice: of Tiberias: a second name for the same lake
decisions.reason: Herod Antipas founded the city of Tiberias on the western shore of the lake in about AD 20 and named it after the emperor Tiberius. In time the lake itself came to be called after the city, and John gives both names, perhaps for readers who knew it by the newer one. He uses the newer name alone in 21:1.

decisions.choice: after these things: a loose link of time, with no length given
alternatives: immediately after the events of chapter 5
decisions.reason: John often moves on to a new episode with this phrase (3:22; 5:1; 7:1). Chapter 5 took place in Jerusalem and this one in Galilee, and John does not say how much time passed between them or how Jesus came back north.

decisions.choice: across the sea: to the other shore of the Lake of Galilee
decisions.reason: The word means "sea", but here it is the freshwater lake of Galilee, about 13 miles (21 km) long. John does not say which shore Jesus reached. The boats from Tiberias in verse 23 and the return to Capernaum in verses 17 and 24 suggest a quieter place away from the towns of the western and northern shores; Luke 9:10 places the feeding near Bethsaida.

decisions.choice: [the Sea] of Tiberias (L); which is also called the Sea of Tiberias (B); This large lake was also called (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek simply adds the second name. Literal brackets the words needed to make it read as a name of the same lake; Balanced and Readable say plainly that it is a second name (meaning decision m1), and Readable says that this "sea" is a lake.

decisions.choice: [el mar] de Tiberíades (L); que también se llama (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in English: the Greek simply adds the second name of the same lake (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἠκολούθει δὲ αὐτῷ ὄχλος πολύς, ὅτι ἐθεώρουν τὰ σημεῖα ἃ ἐποίει ἐπὶ τῶν ἀσθενούντων.

records.literal_gloss: Was following now him a crowd large, because they were seeing the signs which he was doing on the [ones] being sick.

en.L: Now a great crowd was following {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, because they were watching the signs which {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was doing upon those who were sick.
en.B: A large crowd kept following {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, because they kept seeing the signs {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was doing by healing the sick.
en.R: A huge crowd of people kept following {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They had seen the signs {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was doing when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} healed sick people.

es.L: Y lo seguía una gran multitud, porque veían las señales que hacía en los enfermos.
es.B: Una gran multitud lo seguía, porque veía las señales que hacía al sanar a los enfermos.
es.R: Muchísima gente lo seguía. Habían visto las señales que hacía cuando sanaba a los enfermos.

decisions.choice: was following, were seeing, was doing: ongoing action
decisions.reason: All three verbs describe something that went on over a period: the crowd kept following him, because they kept seeing the signs he kept doing.

decisions.choice: signs: deeds of power that point to who Jesus is; here, healings of the sick
decisions.reason: John calls Jesus's deeds "signs" because they point beyond themselves (2:11; 20:30-31). The ones meant here are healings, done "on" the sick, such as those at 4:46-54 and 5:1-9.

decisions.choice: the crowd follows because of the signs, not yet because it understands them
decisions.reason: John often shows people drawn by the signs without grasping what they point to (2:23-25). Jesus says this of this very crowd the next day: they looked for him because they ate the bread, not because they saw signs (6:26).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "you" when people speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: by healing the sick (B); when he healed sick people (R)
decisions.reason: "Doing signs on the sick" means healing them (meaning decision m2); Balanced and Readable say so.

decisions.choice: al sanar a los enfermos (B); cuando sanaba (R)
decisions.reason: As in English: "doing signs on the sick" means healing them (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ἀνῆλθεν δὲ εἰς τὸ ὄρος Ἰησοῦς, καὶ ἐκεῖ ἐκάθητο μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Went up now into the mountain Jesus, and there was sitting with the disciples of him.

en.L: And Jesus went up onto the mountain, and there {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was sitting with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples.
en.B: Jesus climbed up into the hills and sat there with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples.
en.R: Jesus went up into the hills and sat down there with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples.

es.L: Y subió Jesús al monte, y allí estaba sentado con sus discípulos.
es.B: Jesús subió al monte y se sentó allí con sus discípulos.
es.R: Jesús subió al monte y se sentó allí con sus discípulos.

decisions.choice: the mountain: the hill country rising from the shore of the lake
decisions.reason: The word can mean a mountain or the hills in general. The article probably points to the hills by the lake rather than a named peak; no mountain is named, and the crowd can reach the place on foot (verse 5).

decisions.choice: going up the mountain: a possible echo of Moses
decisions.reason: The chapter is set near Passover (verse 4) and soon compares Jesus with Moses and the manna (6:14, 31-32). Moses went up the mountain to meet God (Exodus 19:3; 24:12-18), and some readers hear an echo. The words are also an ordinary description of the scene, so the echo is possible but not certain.

decisions.choice: sitting: the posture of a teacher with his disciples
decisions.reason: Teachers in Israel sat to teach (Matthew 5:1; Luke 4:20). The imperfect tense pictures Jesus settled there with the disciples when the crowd arrives.

decisions.choice: the hills
decisions.reason: "The mountain" suggests one peak; Balanced and Readable say "hills" for the hill country by the lake (meaning decision m1). Verse 15 uses the same word the same way.

decisions.choice: el monte
decisions.reason: English says "hills" because "the mountain" suggests one peak. Spanish "monte" covers hill country as well (meaning decision m1), so every level keeps it, and with it the possible echo of Moses (m2).

source.text: ἦν δὲ ἐγγὺς τὸ πάσχα, ἡ ἑορτὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων.

records.literal_gloss: Was now near the Passover, the feast of the Jews.

en.L: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.
en.B: It was nearly time for Passover, the Jewish festival.
en.R: It was almost time for Passover. This was the Jewish festival when people remembered how God had set Israel free from Egypt.

es.L: Y estaba cerca la Pascua, la fiesta de los judíos.
es.B: Se acercaba la Pascua, la fiesta judía.
es.R: Faltaba poco para la Pascua. Era la fiesta judía en que el pueblo recordaba cómo Dios había liberado a Israel de Egipto.

decisions.choice: Passover: the spring festival that remembered the exodus from Egypt
decisions.reason: Passover was kept in the spring, in the month of Nisan (Exodus 12). It is the second of three Passovers John mentions (2:13; 11:55), and it explains why there was plenty of green grass in verse 10. Jesus is not said to go up to Jerusalem for it.

decisions.choice: the note about Passover sets the feeding and the teaching that follows in the light of the exodus
decisions.reason: What follows recalls Israel's escape from Egypt: bread given in a lonely place, a prophet like Moses (verse 14), a crossing of the sea (verses 16-21), and the talk of manna and the true bread from heaven (6:31-35). At the final Passover Jesus dies as the Lamb of God (1:29; 19:14, 36). John mentions the festival here to point the reader that way.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people, whose festival it was
decisions.reason: As at 2:13 and 5:1, John names the festival as the people's, for readers who did not keep it.

decisions.choice: the Jewish festival
decisions.reason: Here the word means the Jewish people (meaning decision m3), so Balanced and Readable say "Jewish" without naming the leaders.

decisions.choice: when people remembered how God had set Israel free from Egypt
decisions.reason: Readable explains what Passover was, since the passage depends on it (meaning decisions m1 and m2).

decisions.choice: la fiesta judía
decisions.reason: Here the word means the Jewish people (meaning decision m3), so no level speaks of leaders.

decisions.choice: en que el pueblo recordaba cómo Dios había liberado a Israel de Egipto
decisions.reason: As in English: Readable explains Passover, since the passage depends on it.

source.text: ἐπάρας οὖν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ θεασάμενος ὅτι πολὺς ὄχλος ἔρχεται πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγει πρὸς Φίλιππον· Πόθεν ἀγοράσωμεν ἄρτους ἵνα φάγωσιν οὗτοι;

records.literal_gloss: Having lifted up then the eyes the Jesus and having seen that a large crowd is coming toward him, says to Philip, "From where may we buy loaves so that may eat these?"

en.L: So Jesus, lifting up {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} eyes and seeing that a great crowd is coming toward {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, says to Philip, "From where are we to buy loaves, so that these [people] may eat?"
en.B: Jesus looked up and saw that a large crowd was making its way toward {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked Philip, "Where are we going to buy bread to feed these people?"
en.R: Jesus looked up and saw a big crowd coming to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He asked Philip, "Where can we buy bread so that all these people can eat?"

es.L: Entonces Jesús, alzando los ojos y viendo que una gran multitud viene hacia {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}}, dice a Felipe: «¿De dónde compraremos panes para que coman estos?».
es.B: Jesús levantó la vista y vio que una gran multitud venía hacia {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}}. Entonces le preguntó a Felipe: «¿Dónde vamos a comprar pan para darles de comer a todos estos?».
es.R: Jesús levantó la vista y vio que mucha gente venía hacia {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}}. Le preguntó a Felipe: «¿Dónde podemos comprar pan para que coma toda esta gente?».

decisions.choice: lifting up his eyes: looking up and taking notice
decisions.reason: The phrase is a Hebrew way of saying that someone looked up attentively at what was before him (Genesis 18:2; John 4:35; 17:1).

decisions.choice: from where are we to buy bread: a question that recalls Moses in the wilderness
decisions.reason: "From where" asks about the source, not just the shop. In the wilderness Moses asked God, "Where am I to get meat to give to all this people?" (Numbers 11:13). In this Passover setting (verse 4) the question echoes his; the answer is that the bread will come from Jesus himself. By saying "we", Jesus draws the disciples into the problem.

decisions.choice: Philip: a disciple from Bethsaida, near the place
decisions.reason: Philip came from Bethsaida (1:44), a town at the north end of the lake, so he was a natural person to ask about where food could be found nearby.

decisions.choice: asked
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he says", "they see") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage (verses 5, 8, 12, 19 and 20).

decisions.choice: bread
decisions.reason: The word means loaves: flat, round breads that were the basic food of every meal. Balanced and Readable say "bread" here; verse 9 counts them as loaves.

decisions.choice: historic present at Literal; pretérito at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in John: Literal keeps John's present ("dice", "ven"); Balanced and Readable use the pretérito. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: ¿De dónde ...? (L); ¿Dónde ...? (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "de dónde", which asks about the source and recalls Moses's question (meaning decision m2).

source.text: τοῦτο δὲ ἔλεγεν πειράζων αὐτόν, αὐτὸς γὰρ ᾔδει τί ἔμελλεν ποιεῖν.

records.literal_gloss: This now he was saying testing him, he himself for knew what he was about to do.

en.L: Now {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying this to test him, for {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} knew what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was about to do.
en.B: Jesus said this to test Philip; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} already knew what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was going to do.
en.R: Jesus asked this to test Philip. Jesus already knew what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was going to do.

es.L: Pero esto decía para probarlo, porque {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} mismo sabía lo que iba a hacer.
es.B: Jesús dijo esto para poner a prueba a Felipe; {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} ya sabía lo que iba a hacer.
es.R: Jesús le preguntó esto para poner a prueba a Felipe. Jesús ya sabía lo que iba a hacer.

decisions.choice: testing: drawing out Philip's understanding and trust
decisions.reason: The verb can mean either to test or to tempt. Here Jesus does not lead Philip into wrong; he gives him the chance to show whether he will look to Jesus for what is needed. In the exodus story God "tested" Israel with the manna (Exodus 16:4).

decisions.choice: for he himself knew: a comment by the narrator
decisions.reason: John steps in to explain that the question was not because Jesus did not know what to do. He often notes what Jesus knew beforehand (2:24-25; 6:64; 13:1-3).

decisions.choice: Jesus ... Philip
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name both men, since "he" and "him" refer to different people in this short sentence.

decisions.choice: Jesús ... Felipe
decisions.reason: As in English: Balanced and Readable name both men.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ Φίλιππος· Διακοσίων δηναρίων ἄρτοι οὐκ ἀρκοῦσιν αὐτοῖς ἵνα ἕκαστος βραχύ τι λάβῃ.

records.literal_gloss: Answered him Philip, "Of two hundred denarii loaves not are enough for them, so that each a little something may receive."

en.L: Philip answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Two hundred denarii [worth] of loaves are not enough for them, for each to receive a little something."
en.B: Philip answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Bread costing {{units:more than half a year's wages|two hundred denarii}} would not go far enough to give each of them even a little."
en.R: Philip answered, "Even if we spent {{units:more than half a year's pay|two hundred denarii}} on bread, there would not be enough for each person to have a small piece."

es.L: Le respondió Felipe: «Doscientos denarios de pan no bastan para que cada uno reciba un poco».
es.B: Felipe le respondió: «Ni con pan por valor de {{units:más de medio año de salario|doscientos denarios}} alcanzaría para darle un poco a cada uno».
es.R: Felipe le respondió: «Aunque gastáramos {{units:más de medio año de sueldo|doscientos denarios}} en pan, no alcanzaría para que cada uno comiera un pedacito».

decisions.choice: two hundred denarii: about two hundred days' wages
decisions.reason: A denarius was a silver coin, the usual pay for a laborer's day of work (Matthew 20:2). Two hundred denarii was the pay for more than half a year of working days, far more than a group of traveling disciples would carry.

decisions.choice: are not enough: Philip counts the cost and finds the task impossible
decisions.reason: Jesus asked where bread could come from; Philip answers with what it would cost, and even that sum would give each person only a taste. The answer shows that he is looking for a way that does not depend on Jesus (verse 6).

decisions.choice: {{units:more than half a year's wages|two hundred denarii}} (B); {{units:more than half a year's pay|two hundred denarii}} (R)
decisions.reason: The coin means nothing to most readers, so Balanced and Readable give its value in wages by default, and the units setting shows the original "two hundred denarii". Literal always keeps the coin.

decisions.choice: Two hundred denarii [worth] of loaves
decisions.reason: The Greek says "loaves of two hundred denarii", meaning loaves costing that much; Literal brackets the word needed to say so.

decisions.choice: {{units:más de medio año de salario|doscientos denarios}}
decisions.reason: As in English: the coin means nothing to most readers, so Balanced and Readable give its value in wages by default (meaning decision m1); the units setting shows the original.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ εἷς ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, Ἀνδρέας ὁ ἀδελφὸς Σίμωνος Πέτρου·

records.literal_gloss: Says to him one of the disciples of him, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter,

en.L: One of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}},
en.B: Then Andrew, one of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples and the brother of Simon Peter, said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}},
en.R: Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, was another of the disciples. He said to Jesus,

es.L: Le dice uno de sus discípulos, Andrés, el hermano de Simón Pedro:
es.B: Entonces Andrés, uno de sus discípulos y hermano de Simón Pedro, le dijo:
es.R: Andrés, el hermano de Simón Pedro, era otro de los discípulos. Le dijo a Jesús:

decisions.choice: Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter: one of the first disciples, from the same town as Philip
decisions.reason: Andrew was among the first to follow Jesus, and he brought his brother Simon to him (1:40-42). He and Philip both came from Bethsaida (1:44), and they appear together again at 12:22. Here once more Andrew brings someone to Jesus.

decisions.choice: one of his disciples: a second disciple, besides Philip, speaks
decisions.reason: Jesus put the question to Philip, but Andrew joins in with what he has found; the speech itself follows in the next sentence.

decisions.choice: He said to Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the introduction into two short sentences and names Jesus as the one Andrew speaks to.

source.text: Ἔστιν παιδάριον ὧδε ὃς ἔχει πέντε ἄρτους κριθίνους καὶ δύο ὀψάρια· ἀλλὰ ταῦτα τί ἐστιν εἰς τοσούτους;

records.literal_gloss: "There is a little boy here who has five loaves barley and two fish; but these what are for so many?"

en.L: "A little boy is here who has five loaves of barley and two small fish; but these, what are [they] for so many?"
en.B: "There is a young boy here who has five loaves of barley bread and two small fish. But what good is that with so many people?"
en.R: "A boy here has five small loaves of barley bread and two little fish. But that will not help much with so many people!"

es.L: «Aquí hay un muchachito que tiene cinco panes de cebada y dos pescados pequeños; pero ¿qué es esto para tantos?».
es.B: «Aquí hay un muchacho que tiene cinco panes de cebada y dos pescaditos. Pero ¿de qué sirve eso para tanta gente?».
es.R: «Aquí hay un muchacho que tiene cinco panecitos de cebada y dos pescaditos. ¡Pero eso no alcanza para tanta gente!».

decisions.choice: a little boy: a child or a young lad
decisions.reason: The word is a diminutive of the word for a child, and can also mean a young servant. Nothing here says he was a servant; he is simply a boy in the crowd who has some food with him. His exact age is not given.

decisions.choice: barley loaves: the cheap bread of poor people
decisions.reason: Barley was cheaper than wheat and was the usual bread of the poor (compare Revelation 6:6, where barley costs a third the price of wheat). Only John says the loaves were barley.

decisions.choice: barley loaves for a crowd: an echo of Elisha
decisions.reason: In 2 Kings 4:42-44 a man brings the prophet Elisha twenty barley loaves; his servant asks how that can feed a hundred men, and the men eat and have some left over, as the LORD had said. Here barley loaves, the question "what are these for so many?" and the leftovers (verses 12-13) follow the same pattern, on a far greater scale.

decisions.choice: fish: small fish, eaten with bread
decisions.reason: The word is a diminutive and was used of fish prepared to eat with bread, often dried or salted. Fish from the lake were salted and traded around Galilee.

decisions.choice: small fish (L, B); little fish (R)
decisions.reason: Every level shows that these were small fish (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: what good is that with so many people? (B); that will not help much with so many people! (R)
alternatives: what are these for so many? (Literal)
decisions.reason: Andrew's question expects the answer "nothing"; Balanced asks it in everyday words and Readable states what it means.

decisions.choice: dos pescados pequeños (L); dos pescaditos (B, R)
decisions.reason: Every level shows that these were small fish, prepared to eat with bread (meaning decision m4).

source.text: εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ποιήσατε τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἀναπεσεῖν.

records.literal_gloss: Said the Jesus, "Make the people to recline."

en.L: Jesus said, "Make the {{gender:people|men}} recline."
en.B: Jesus said, "Tell the {{gender:people|men}} to sit down."
en.R: Jesus said, "Tell everyone to sit down."

es.L: Dijo Jesús: «{{plural_you:Hagan|Haced}} recostar a {{gender:las personas|los hombres}}».
es.B: Jesús dijo: «{{plural_you:Hagan|Haced}} que {{gender:las personas|los hombres}} se sienten».
es.R: Jesús dijo: «{{plural_you:Díganles|Decidles}} a todos que se sienten».

decisions.choice: recline: settle on the ground for a meal
decisions.reason: At a meal people reclined, leaning on one elbow (13:23). On a hillside this meant sitting or lying on the grass. The word tells the crowd that they are about to be fed.

decisions.choice: the people: the whole crowd, men and women
decisions.reason: This word means human beings in general. When John counts them in the next sentence, he uses a different word that means men specifically.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The word is inclusive (meaning decision m2), so the default is "people"; the gender setting gives the traditional "men". Readable says "everyone", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: sit down
decisions.reason: "Recline" sounds like a couch; on a grassy hillside "sit down" says what the people did.

decisions.choice: {{gender:las personas|los hombres}}
decisions.reason: The word means people in general (meaning decision m2). "Las personas" keeps the plural verb in both forms; Readable says "todos".

decisions.choice: ustedes / vosotros forms
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks to the disciples, so each plural "you" and its verb is the reader setting: ustedes (Latin America, the default) or vosotros (Spain). This applies throughout the chapter.

source.text: ἦν δὲ χόρτος πολὺς ἐν τῷ τόπῳ.

records.literal_gloss: Was now grass much in the place.

en.L: Now much grass was in that place.
en.B: Grass grew thickly in that spot.
en.R: The ground there was covered with grass.

es.L: Y había mucha hierba en aquel lugar.
es.B: En aquel lugar había mucha hierba.
es.R: El suelo allí estaba cubierto de hierba.

decisions.choice: much grass: the hills were green in spring
decisions.reason: Passover was near (verse 4), at the end of the rainy season, when the hills of Galilee are green; later in the year the grass is dry and brown. The detail fits the season John has named.

decisions.choice: much grass: possibly an echo of the shepherd who makes his flock lie down in green pastures
alternatives: a detail of the scene only
decisions.reason: Psalm 23:2 pictures the LORD as a shepherd who makes his sheep lie down in green pastures, and Jesus will call himself the good shepherd (10:11). Some readers see that picture here, as the people lie down and are fed. John does not point it out.

source.text: ἀνέπεσαν οὖν οἱ ἄνδρες τὸν ἀριθμὸν ὡς πεντακισχίλιοι.

records.literal_gloss: Reclined then the men the number about five thousand.

en.L: So the men reclined, in number about 5,000.
en.B: So the men sat down, about 5,000 of them.
en.R: So the men sat down. There were about 5,000 of them.

es.L: Se recostaron, pues, los hombres, en número de unos 5000.
es.B: Así que los hombres se sentaron; eran unos 5000.
es.R: Entonces los hombres se sentaron. Eran unos 5000.

decisions.choice: the men: adult males, the ones who were counted
alternatives: the whole crowd, men and women together
decisions.reason: John changes from the general word for people (the first sentence of this verse) to the word for men. It was usual to count the men of a gathering (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 1:2-3). Matthew 14:21 says that women and children were there besides; John gives only the number of men.

decisions.choice: about five thousand: a round figure
decisions.reason: "About" shows that this is an estimate, not an exact count.
Numbers above ninety-nine are written in numerals at every level.

decisions.choice: sat down
decisions.reason: As in the first sentence of this verse.

decisions.choice: los hombres, no gender setting
decisions.reason: Here John uses the word for men, the adult males who were counted (meaning decision m1), so "los hombres" is not under the setting. Spanish writes four-digit numbers without a separator.

source.text: ἔλαβεν οὖν τοὺς ἄρτους ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ εὐχαριστήσας διέδωκεν τοῖς ἀνακειμένοις, ὁμοίως καὶ ἐκ τῶν ὀψαρίων ὅσον ἤθελον.

records.literal_gloss: Took then the loaves the Jesus and having given thanks distributed to the [ones] reclining, likewise also from the fish as much as they were wanting.

en.L: So Jesus took the loaves, and after giving thanks {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} handed [them] out to those reclining; in the same way also from the fish, as much as they were wanting.
en.B: So Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and shared them out among the people sitting there, and the fish too, as much as anyone wanted.
en.R: Jesus took the loaves and thanked God for them. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave the bread to the people who were sitting there. He gave out the fish in the same way. Everyone had as much as they wanted.

es.L: Tomó, pues, Jesús los panes y, habiendo dado gracias, los repartió a los que estaban recostados; y de igual manera de los pescados, cuanto querían.
es.B: Entonces Jesús tomó los panes, dio gracias y los repartió entre los que estaban sentados, y lo mismo hizo con los pescados, todo lo que quisieron.
es.R: Jesús tomó los panes y le dio gracias a Dios por ellos. Luego repartió el pan entre la gente que estaba sentada. Hizo lo mismo con los pescados. Todos comieron cuanto quisieron.

decisions.choice: having given thanks: the blessing said over bread before a meal
decisions.reason: Before a meal the head of the household took the bread and gave thanks to God for it. Jesus does what any Jewish host would do, and John recalls it again in 6:23: "where they ate the bread after the Lord had given thanks".

decisions.choice: gave thanks: an ordinary meal blessing, with a possible echo of the Lord's Supper
alternatives: a deliberate picture of the Lord's Supper
decisions.reason: This verb, which gave the Lord's Supper its later name, the Eucharist, is used when Jesus gives thanks over the bread at the Last Supper (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24). John tells no such scene at the supper, and later in this chapter Jesus speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood (6:51-58). Readers who knew the church's meal could hear an echo in "took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed". But the words are also the normal way to describe a Jewish meal, and the text does not make the link itself.

decisions.choice: he distributed to those reclining (SBLGNT): Jesus himself hands out the food
alternatives: he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those reclining (later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add that Jesus gave the bread to the disciples and they gave it to the people, as Matthew 14:19, Mark 6:41 and Luke 9:16 say. The earliest manuscripts do not have these words, and they look like an addition to bring John into line with the other Gospels. In John's text the gift comes straight from Jesus's hands. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: as much as they wanted: there was no rationing
decisions.reason: Philip expected each to get only a little (verse 7); instead each one had as much as he wanted, and there was more left over (verses 12-13).

decisions.choice: thanked God for them
decisions.reason: Readable says to whom the thanks were given, which the Greek takes for granted (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: shared them out (B); gave (R)
decisions.reason: Everyday words for giving each person a share.

decisions.choice: le dio gracias a Dios por ellos
decisions.reason: As in English: Readable says to whom the thanks were given (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ὡς δὲ ἐνεπλήσθησαν λέγει τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ· Συναγάγετε τὰ περισσεύσαντα κλάσματα, ἵνα μή τι ἀπόληται.

records.literal_gloss: When now they were filled, he says to the disciples of him, "Gather the having been left over fragments, so that not anything may be lost."

en.L: And when they were filled, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, "Gather the broken pieces that are left over, so that not anything may be lost."
en.B: Once they were all full, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} told {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, "Pick up the broken pieces that remain, so that nothing is lost."
en.R: When everyone was full, Jesus told {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, "Pick up all the pieces of food that are left. Do not let any of it be lost."

es.L: Y cuando se saciaron, dice a sus discípulos: «{{plural_you:Recojan|Recoged}} los pedazos que sobraron, para que no se pierda nada».
es.B: Cuando todos quedaron satisfechos, les dijo a sus discípulos: «{{plural_you:Recojan|Recoged}} los pedazos que sobraron, para que no se pierda nada».
es.R: Cuando todos estuvieron llenos, Jesús les dijo a sus discípulos: «{{plural_you:Recojan|Recoged}} todos los pedazos que sobraron. Que no se pierda nada».

decisions.choice: they were filled: they had eaten until they were satisfied
decisions.reason: The verb means to be filled full. The point is plenty, set against Philip's "each a little" (verse 7).

decisions.choice: fragments: pieces broken off the loaves
decisions.reason: The word means broken pieces. These are the pieces broken off for the people and not eaten, not scraps they had dropped.

decisions.choice: so that nothing may be lost: not to waste the food, with an echo of Jesus losing none of those given to him
alternatives: only a matter of not wasting food
decisions.reason: The plain sense is not to waste good food. But the same verb is used in this chapter for what Jesus will not let happen to those the Father gives him: "that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me" (6:39; also 3:16; 17:12; 18:9). John may want the reader to hear that echo. In the exodus story the manna could not be kept and spoiled (Exodus 16:19-20); this bread is gathered up.

decisions.choice: told
decisions.reason: The historic present; see the note at verse 5.

decisions.choice: be lost (L, R); is lost (B)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps "lost", so that the echo of 6:39 noted in meaning decision m3 stays visible.

decisions.choice: perder
decisions.reason: Every level uses "perder" for this verb here, in 6:27 ("la comida que se pierde") and in 6:39 ("que no pierda nada"), so the echo noted in meaning decision m3 stays visible.

source.text: συνήγαγον οὖν, καὶ ἐγέμισαν δώδεκα κοφίνους κλασμάτων ἐκ τῶν πέντε ἄρτων τῶν κριθίνων ἃ ἐπερίσσευσαν τοῖς βεβρωκόσιν.

records.literal_gloss: They gathered then, and filled twelve baskets of fragments from the five loaves the barley which were left over to the [ones] having eaten.

en.L: So they gathered [them] and filled twelve baskets of pieces from the five loaves of barley, which were more than those who had eaten [needed].
en.B: They did so, and from the five barley loaves they filled twelve baskets with the pieces that remained after everyone had eaten.
en.R: So the disciples gathered the pieces. They filled twelve baskets with what was left from the five barley loaves after everyone had eaten.

es.L: Los recogieron, pues, y llenaron doce cestas de pedazos de los cinco panes de cebada, que sobraron a los que habían comido.
es.B: Así lo hicieron, y con los pedazos de los cinco panes de cebada que sobraron después de que todos comieron llenaron doce cestas.
es.R: Entonces los discípulos recogieron los pedazos. Llenaron doce cestas con lo que sobró de los cinco panes de cebada después de que todos comieron.

decisions.choice: baskets: good-sized baskets of the kind travelers carried
decisions.reason: This is the word for a stout wicker basket used for carrying food and goods. Twelve full baskets is far more than the five loaves the meal began with.

decisions.choice: twelve: possibly pointing to the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve disciples
alternatives: a count with no further meaning
decisions.reason: There may simply have been one basket for each of the twelve disciples (6:67-70). The number twelve also stands for the people of Israel, and some readers see a sign that Jesus provides for all God's people. John does not draw that out.

decisions.choice: which were left over to those who had eaten: the surplus beyond what the people ate
decisions.reason: The pieces were more than the people needed, as in Elisha's feeding, where "they ate and had some left" (2 Kings 4:44).

decisions.choice: gathered [them]; more than ... [needed]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words English needs to complete the two phrases.

decisions.choice: the disciples
decisions.reason: Readable names who did the gathering (verse 12).

decisions.choice: no supplied words (L)
decisions.reason: Spanish can say "los recogieron" and "que sobraron a los que habían comido" as the Greek does, so Literal needs none of the English brackets.

source.text: οἱ οὖν ἄνθρωποι ἰδόντες ὃ ἐποίησεν σημεῖον ἔλεγον ὅτι Οὗτός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ προφήτης ὁ ἐρχόμενος εἰς τὸν κόσμον.

records.literal_gloss: The then people having seen what he did sign were saying, "This is truly the prophet the [one] coming into the world."

en.L: So the {{gender:people|men}}, having seen the sign that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did, were saying, "This is truly the Prophet who is coming into the world."
en.B: The {{gender:people|men}} who had seen the sign {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did kept saying, "This really is the Prophet, the one who is coming into the world!"
en.R: The {{gender:people|men}} saw this sign that Jesus had done. They said, "This man really must be the Prophet whom God promised to send into the world!"

es.L: Entonces {{gender:las personas|los hombres}}, al ver la señal que había hecho, decían: «Este es verdaderamente el Profeta que viene al mundo».
es.B: {{gender:Las personas|Los hombres}} que vieron la señal que hizo decían: «¡Este es de verdad el Profeta, el que viene al mundo!».
es.R: {{gender:Las personas|Los hombres}} vieron esta señal que Jesús había hecho, y decían: «¡De verdad este hombre tiene que ser el Profeta que Dios prometió enviar al mundo!».

decisions.choice: the sign that he did, singular (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the signs that he did, plural (some manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have the plural, "signs", perhaps under the influence of verse 2. The singular, pointing to the feeding just done, is the better-supported reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Prophet: the prophet like Moses whom God promised to raise up
alternatives: a prophet in a general sense
decisions.reason: In Deuteronomy 18:15-18 Moses tells Israel that God will raise up a prophet like him. In John's day people looked for this Prophet (1:21, 25; 7:40). After bread given in a lonely place, as Moses' people received manna, the crowd draws the comparison. The comparison is right as far as it goes, but Jesus will say that it was not Moses who gave the bread from heaven (6:32).

decisions.choice: coming into the world: the expected one who comes from God to humanity; world means the world of people
decisions.reason: "The one coming" was a way of speaking of the one God would send (11:27; Matthew 11:3). "The world" here is the world of human beings, to whom he comes, as at 1:9 and 3:19.

decisions.choice: were saying: the imperfect shows the talk spreading through the crowd
decisions.reason: The tense pictures people saying it to one another, which leads to the plan in verse 15.

decisions.choice: the Prophet, with a capital
decisions.reason: A capital shows that the crowd means one particular expected figure (meaning decision m2), not any prophet.

decisions.choice: whom God promised to send
decisions.reason: Readable explains which prophet is meant (Deuteronomy 18:15-18). The crowd knew the promise, so this does not put anything in their mouths that they did not know.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The general word for people, as in verse 10; the gender setting gives the traditional "men".

decisions.choice: {{gender:las personas|los hombres}}
decisions.reason: The general word for people, as in verse 10.

decisions.choice: que Dios prometió enviar
decisions.reason: As in English: Readable explains which prophet is meant (meaning decision m2).

source.text: Ἰησοῦς οὖν γνοὺς ὅτι μέλλουσιν ἔρχεσθαι καὶ ἁρπάζειν αὐτὸν ἵνα ποιήσωσιν βασιλέα ἀνεχώρησεν πάλιν εἰς τὸ ὄρος αὐτὸς μόνος.

records.literal_gloss: Jesus then having known that they are about to come and to seize him so that they may make [him] king, withdrew again into the mountain he himself alone.

en.L: So Jesus, knowing that they were about to come and seize {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in order to make [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] king, withdrew again to the mountain, alone by {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}.
en.B: Jesus realized that they were about to come and carry {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} off to make {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} king, so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went back up into the hills, alone.
en.R: Jesus knew that the people were planning to grab {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and force {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to be their king. So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} slipped away again, up into the hills, all by {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}.

es.L: Entonces Jesús, sabiendo que iban a venir para llevárselo a la fuerza y hacerlo rey, se retiró otra vez al monte, {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} solo.
es.B: Jesús se dio cuenta de que iban a venir a llevárselo a la fuerza para hacerlo rey, así que se retiró de nuevo al monte, {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} solo.
es.R: Jesús sabía que la gente pensaba agarrarlo y obligarlo a ser su rey. Por eso se fue otra vez al monte, completamente solo.

decisions.choice: seize: take by force
decisions.reason: The verb means to snatch or carry off by force. The crowd means to make him king whether he wishes it or not.

decisions.choice: make him king: the hope for a leader who would free Israel from Rome
decisions.reason: Many in Galilee hoped for a king like David who would drive out the Romans; a prophet like Moses who fed the people seemed just such a leader. Jesus refuses this kind of kingship. He is a king, but his kingdom is not from this world (18:36-37).

decisions.choice: knowing: Jesus knew their plan before they acted
decisions.reason: John does not say how Jesus knew; he often notes that Jesus knew what was in people (2:24-25).

decisions.choice: again to the mountain: back to the hills of verse 3
decisions.reason: "Again" looks back to verse 3. Jesus had been in the hills with his disciples; now he goes back up alone, leaving the disciples behind (verse 16).

decisions.choice: the hills
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

decisions.choice: el monte
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

source.text: Ὡς δὲ ὀψία ἐγένετο κατέβησαν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν, καὶ ἐμβάντες εἰς πλοῖον ἤρχοντο πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης εἰς Καφαρναούμ.

records.literal_gloss: When now evening came went down the disciples of him to the sea, \v 17 and having embarked into a boat they were going across the sea to Capernaum.

en.L: Now as evening came on, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples went down to the sea, \v 17 and having stepped into a boat, they were heading across the sea to Capernaum.
en.B: At evening {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples went down to the shore. \v 17 They boarded a boat and were making their way over the sea to Capernaum.
en.R: That evening, Jesus's disciples went down to the lake. \v 17 They got into a boat and started across the lake to the town of Capernaum.

es.L: Al llegar la tarde, sus discípulos bajaron al mar, \v 17 y, subiendo a una barca, iban al otro lado del mar, hacia Capernaúm.
es.B: Al anochecer, sus discípulos bajaron a la orilla. \v 17 Subieron a una barca y cruzaban el mar hacia Capernaúm.
es.R: Esa tarde, los discípulos de Jesús bajaron al lago. \v 17 Subieron a una barca y empezaron a cruzar el lago hacia el pueblo de Capernaúm.

decisions.choice: Capernaum: a town on the northwest shore, where Jesus often stayed
decisions.reason: Capernaum was a fishing town on the northern shore of the lake (2:12). The crowd looks for Jesus there the next day (6:24), and he teaches there in the synagogue (6:59).

decisions.choice: they were going: the crossing had begun but was not finished
decisions.reason: The imperfect describes a journey under way. It sets the scene for what happens on the water.

decisions.choice: evening: late in the day, toward dusk
decisions.reason: The word covers late afternoon and the beginning of night. By the next sentence it is fully dark.

decisions.choice: the lake
decisions.reason: The Greek word is "sea". Literal and Balanced keep it, so the thread of the sea through the passage stays visible; Readable says "lake", which is what it was (see verse 1).

decisions.choice: Jesus's disciples; the town of
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, who has been off alone since the last sentence, and says that Capernaum was a town.

decisions.choice: el mar (L, B); el lago (R)
decisions.reason: As in English: Literal and Balanced keep "mar", the Greek word; Readable says "lago" so young readers do not picture the ocean.

source.text: καὶ σκοτία ἤδη ἐγεγόνει καὶ οὔπω ἐληλύθει πρὸς αὐτοὺς ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ἥ τε θάλασσα ἀνέμου μεγάλου πνέοντος διεγείρετο.

records.literal_gloss: And darkness already had come and not yet had come to them the Jesus, \v 18 the and sea, a wind great blowing, was being stirred up.

en.L: And darkness had already come, and Jesus had not yet come to them; \v 18 and the sea was being stirred up, a great wind blowing.
en.B: Darkness had already fallen, and still Jesus had not come out to them. \v 18 The sea was getting rough, whipped up by a strong wind.
en.R: It was already dark, and Jesus had not come to them yet. \v 18 A strong wind was blowing, and the lake was getting very rough.

es.L: Y ya había oscurecido, y Jesús todavía no había venido a ellos; \v 18 y el mar se agitaba, porque soplaba un fuerte viento.
es.B: Ya había oscurecido, y Jesús aún no se había reunido con ellos. \v 18 El mar se estaba encrespando, agitado por un viento fuerte.
es.R: Ya era de noche, y Jesús todavía no había llegado adonde estaban ellos. \v 18 Soplaba un viento fuerte, y el lago se estaba poniendo muy agitado.

decisions.choice: had not yet come to them: the disciples were without Jesus, and the reader is told he will come
alternatives: they had arranged to pick him up on the way
decisions.reason: "Not yet" suggests that his coming was expected, at least by the narrator. John does not say whether the disciples had agreed to meet him; the words prepare for verse 19.

decisions.choice: darkness: night had fallen, with a possible hint of John's theme of darkness
decisions.reason: John uses this word for the darkness that cannot overcome the light (1:5; 8:12; 12:35, 46). Here it means plainly that night had come; the disciples in the dark without Jesus may also be a picture of that theme, but this is not stated.

decisions.choice: was being stirred up: the waves were growing because a strong wind was blowing
decisions.reason: The imperfect pictures the sea becoming rougher; the participle about the wind gives the cause. Sudden strong winds come down on the lake from the hills around it.

decisions.choice: The sea was getting rough, whipped up by a strong wind (B); A strong wind was blowing, and the lake was getting very rough (R)
alternatives: the sea was being stirred up, a great wind blowing (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the wind the plain cause of the rough water, as the Greek participle implies.

source.text: ἐληλακότες οὖν ὡς σταδίους εἴκοσι πέντε ἢ τριάκοντα θεωροῦσιν τὸν Ἰησοῦν περιπατοῦντα ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης καὶ ἐγγὺς τοῦ πλοίου γινόμενον, καὶ ἐφοβήθησαν.

records.literal_gloss: Having rowed then about stadia twenty-five or thirty they see the Jesus walking on the sea and near the boat coming, and they were afraid.

en.L: So when they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they see Jesus walking on the sea and drawing near to the boat, and they became afraid.
en.B: After they had rowed about {{units:3 or 3½ miles|twenty-five or thirty stadia}}, they caught sight of Jesus walking on the sea and getting close to the boat, and fear took hold of them.
en.R: They had rowed about {{units:3 or 3½ miles|twenty-five or thirty stadia}} when they saw Jesus walking on top of the water toward the boat. They were frightened.

es.L: Cuando habían remado unos veinticinco o treinta estadios, ven a Jesús caminando sobre el mar y acercándose a la barca, y tuvieron miedo.
es.B: Después de remar unos {{units:5 kilómetros|veinticinco o treinta estadios}}, vieron a Jesús que caminaba sobre el mar y se acercaba a la barca, y se llenaron de miedo.
es.R: Habían remado unos {{units:5 kilómetros|veinticinco o treinta estadios}} cuando vieron a Jesús caminando sobre el agua hacia la barca. Tuvieron miedo.

decisions.choice: twenty-five or thirty stadia: about three to three and a half miles
decisions.reason: A stadion was about 600 feet (185 meters), so twenty-five or thirty of them come to about 4.5 to 5.5 kilometers. The lake is about seven miles across at its widest, so the disciples were far out on the water.

decisions.choice: walking on the sea: on the surface of the water
alternatives: walking by the sea, along the shore
decisions.reason: The same words can mean "by the sea" (21:1), and that has been suggested here. But the disciples are miles out, they are afraid, and Jesus comes near the boat; John tells a wonder, as Matthew 14:25 and Mark 6:48 also do.

decisions.choice: walking on the sea: an act the Scriptures give to God alone
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures God is the one who "treads on the waves of the sea" (Job 9:8) and whose "path was through the sea" (Psalm 77:19, at the exodus). With the Passover setting (verse 4) and Jesus's words in verse 20, the scene points to who Jesus is.

decisions.choice: they were afraid: fear at what they saw, not only at the storm
decisions.reason: John does not mention fear of the waves; the disciples are afraid when they see Jesus on the water (compare Mark 6:49-50).

decisions.choice: about {{units:3 or 3½ miles|twenty-five or thirty stadia}}
decisions.reason: The stadion means nothing to most readers, so Balanced and Readable give the distance in miles by default, and the units setting shows the original measure. Numerals are used in measurements. Literal always keeps the ancient unit.

decisions.choice: caught sight of (B); saw (R)
decisions.reason: The historic present; see the note at verse 5.

decisions.choice: unos {{units:5 kilómetros|veinticinco o treinta estadios}}
decisions.reason: A stadion was about 185 meters, so twenty-five or thirty make about 4.5 to 5.5 kilometers (meaning decision m1). Spanish readers measure in kilometers, as at 2:6 with liters; the units setting shows the original.

source.text: ὁ δὲ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἐγώ εἰμι, μὴ φοβεῖσθε.

records.literal_gloss: He but says to them, "I am; not be afraid."

en.L: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to them, "I am [{{deity_pronoun:he|He}}]; do not be afraid."
en.B: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} told them, "It is I. Do not be afraid."
en.R: But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "It is me! Do not be afraid."

es.L: Pero {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} les dice: «Yo soy; no {{plural_you:tengan|tengáis}} miedo».
es.B: Pero {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} les dijo: «Soy yo. No {{plural_you:tengan|tengáis}} miedo».
es.R: Pero {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} les dijo: «¡Soy yo! No {{plural_you:tengan|tengáis}} miedo».

decisions.choice: I am: plainly "it is I", with an echo of the way God names himself
alternatives: the divine name, I AM, as the main sense
only the plain sense, with no echo
decisions.reason: The words have no predicate. To frightened men in a boat at night the plain sense is "it is I", the one you know. But these are also the words with which God speaks of himself in the Greek of Isaiah: "I am" (Isaiah 43:10; 51:12), and in the same chapter, "Do not fear ... when you pass through the waters, I will be with you" (Isaiah 43:1-2). Jesus says them while doing what Scripture gives to God alone (verse 19, meaning decision m3 there). The plain sense is uppermost, and the echo is likely; later in John the bare "I am" carries it more clearly (8:24, 28, 58). Marked uncertain; a footnote gives the bare "I am".

decisions.choice: do not be afraid: stop being afraid
decisions.reason: The present tense with "not" tells them to stop the fear they already have (verse 19). In the Scriptures God and his messengers often say these words when they appear (Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 43:1; Luke 1:30).

decisions.choice: I am [he] (L); It is I (B); It is me (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "I am". Literal brackets the "he" that the plain sense needs, and it takes the deity_pronoun setting as a pronoun for Christ; Balanced and Readable say the plain sense in everyday words. The footnote gives the bare words, so the echo noted in meaning decision m1 stays visible.

decisions.choice: told (B); said (R)
decisions.reason: The historic present; see the note at verse 5.

decisions.choice: Yo soy (L); Soy yo (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Soy yo" is the plain Spanish for "it is me", which is the sense to frightened men in a boat. Literal keeps "Yo soy", which in Spanish is still a complete answer and keeps the echo of God's own words (meaning decision m1), as at 4:26.

source.text: ἤθελον οὖν λαβεῖν αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ πλοῖον, καὶ εὐθέως ἐγένετο τὸ πλοῖον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς εἰς ἣν ὑπῆγον.

records.literal_gloss: They were wanting then to take him into the boat, and immediately came to be the boat at the land to which they were going.

en.L: So they wanted to take {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} into the boat, and at once the boat came to be at the land toward which they were heading.
en.B: Now they wanted to take {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} into the boat, and right away the boat arrived at the land they were heading for.
en.R: Now they were eager to let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} into the boat. Right away, the boat was at the other side of the lake, where they had been going.

es.L: Entonces quisieron recibirlo en la barca, y en seguida la barca llegó a la tierra adonde iban.
es.B: Entonces quisieron recibirlo en la barca, y en ese momento la barca llegó a la orilla adonde se dirigían.
es.R: Entonces quisieron dejarlo subir a la barca. En ese mismo momento la barca llegó al otro lado del lago, adonde iban.

decisions.choice: they wanted to take him in: their fear turned to welcome; John does not say whether he came aboard before they landed
alternatives: they took him into the boat
decisions.reason: The verb means "they wanted" or "they were willing". Mark 6:51 says that Jesus got into the boat. John says only that they wanted to take him in, and then at once they were at land. He may mean that Jesus got in, or that before they could take him in the boat had already arrived.

decisions.choice: immediately at land: part of the wonder, with a possible echo of Psalm 107
alternatives: a natural arrival after more rowing
decisions.reason: "Immediately" makes the arrival sudden, part of what Jesus does, not the end of a long row. Psalm 107:29-30 says of the LORD that he stilled the storm and "brought them to their desired haven". The echo is possible, not certain.

decisions.choice: the other side of the lake, where they had been going
alternatives: the land to which they were going
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that "the land" was the shore they were making for (Capernaum, verse 17).

decisions.choice: al otro lado del lago, adonde iban
decisions.reason: As in English: Readable says plainly that "the land" was the shore they were making for.
